newsitem.title: USA: TI earnings soar on strong sales of new chips.
newsitem.headline: TI earnings soar on strong sales of new chips.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. said Tuesday its second-quarter profits more than tripled, boosted by higher operating margins and strong revenues for its newest computer chips.

The powerful earnings report took Wall Street by surprise. Texas Instruments stock closed up $12, or 12.2 percent, at an all-time high of $109.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the biggest percentage gaingers and one of the most actively traded issues.
The Dallas-based semiconductor giant's second-quarter net income soared to $249 million, or $1.26 a share, from $76 million, or 39 cents a share, in the same period last year.

Its profits from continuing operations and excluding special items jumped to $213 million, or $1.07 a share, from $41 million, or 21 cents a share. Revenues rose 7 percent from $2.4 billion to $2.56 billion.
Industry analysts had forecast earnings per share of only about 87 cents.

Company executives said semiconductor revenues rose 17 percent from the same quarter last year and were 10 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1997. Operating profits from semiconductors rose fourfold from the second quarter of 1996 and 45 percent from the first quarter.

"This was a very good quarter," President and Chief Executive Thomas Engibous said in a statement. "We realise the opportunity for TI is significant, especially as digital signal processing becomes the core element in a growing number of electronic products."
Digital signal processors, or DSPs, are primarily used in wireless communications and the audio and video functions of electronic equipment, and are at the core of TI's strategy.

With the recent sale of its defence, computer notebook and software divisions, semiconductors now account for 80 percent of the company's revenues, and fast-growing DSPs make up more than 40 percent of semiconductor sales.
"We are moving quickly and aggressively to extend our leadership in this rapidly growing market," Engibous said.
Last year's second-quarter results were battered by a sharp decline in prices for dynamic random access memory chips and the chip market so far has struggled to rebound.
Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said DRAM losses narrowed in recent months but that prices dropped again in June and that it was not clear when the volatility would end.
"A lot of people with crystal balls are trying to figure that out. We don't have any idea really," he told Reuters.

Despite the problems with DRAMs, semiconductor orders were 72 percent higher than in the year-ago period. The company said semiconductor orders, excluding memory chips, were also up over the first quarter but gave no further details.
Aylesworth said the global semiconductor market should grow 10 percent this year, and that the DSP segment was growing at a steady rate of 30 percent per year.

TI's operating profit margin, excluding special charges, rose to 13 percent from 2 percent in the second quarter last year, with margins in the semiconductor division up 10 percentage points from the year-ago period and 4 percentage points from the first quarter.

Revenues and profits from operations in TI's materials and controls business rose 5 percent and 46 percent, respectively, in part because of increased demand for radio frequency identification systems. Calculator revenues were up 19 percent from the same period last year.

Second-quarter results included two special pretax items: an operating charge of $44 million for the termination of joint-venture agreements in Thailand, and a $66 million gain from the sale of three TI businesses. They included its software division, bought by Sterling Software for $165 million.
